readerTitle: Your dumplings are a hit at home. Now take them abroad.
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (만두 레스토랑 그룹의 해외 진출, 배달 앱 결정 포함) · 국가, 수치, 인물 모두 설명용
insight: 해외 진출은 한 번의 큰 결정이 아니라 '어디로, 어떻게, 무엇을 바꾸고, 누구와 싸우나'라는 네 가지 결정이 이어진 것이며, 각 결정은 다음 결정의 위험을 줄이도록 내려야 한다.
misconception: 가장 큰 시장에, 본국에서 통한 방식 그대로, 빠르게 들어가는 것이 가장 좋은 해외 진출이다.

sources.text: 시장 간 거리(문화·제도·지리·경제) 개념: Ghemawat, P. (2001). Distance Still Matters. Harvard Business Review.
모든 인물, 국가, 수치는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 시뮬레이션의 모든 수치(매장 12곳, 회원 8만 명, 6개월 성과 수치)는 가상입니다. 6번 카드 비율 확인: 시그니처 만두 60% + 현지 특선 15% + 기타 25% = 100%.
각 결정의 'best'는 이 가상 상황의 조건(작은 이웃 시장, 현지 배달 앱 지배, 강한 현지 경쟁자)에서의 판단입니다. 일반 법칙처럼 읽히지 않도록 7번 카드에서 한계를 밝혔습니다.
프랜차이즈·합작 계약에 관한 특정 국가의 법률 조언은 다루지 않았습니다. 게시 전 문장이 법률 조언처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your dumplings are a hit at home. Now take them abroad.
body: You're Hana. You run 12 dumpling restaurants known for hand-folded dumplings and a fast lunch. Your loyalty app has 80,000 members.
Investors want growth, and home is getting crowded. Over the next four decisions, you'll take the business into a new country. Each choice shapes the next.

image.label: A dumpling restaurant with a suitcase by the door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 손님이 가득한 아늑한 만두 가게 입구 옆에 여행 가방과 접힌 지도가 놓여 있음. 가게 간판에는 글자 없이 만두 아이콘만. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which country first?
body: Your team shortlists three options. Where do you open first?

options.text: The biggest economy on the list: far away, different language, huge lunch market
options.feedback: The prize is large, but you'd face every gap at once: language, rules, suppliers, tastes. Mistakes there are expensive, and you'd have nothing nearby to learn from.

options.text: The neighboring country: a short flight, a similar language, similar tastes, but a smaller market
options.feedback: Less money on the table, but far fewer surprises. You can visit often, reuse some suppliers and learn cheaply before trying a harder market.

options.text: A city abroad where many people from your home country live
options.feedback: You'd get early fans who already know you. But their love can hide whether local customers care, so a full room may mislead you.

cards.title: Say you chose the neighbor. How do you enter?
body: You know your food. You don't know local landlords, suppliers or hiring. How do you open?

options.text: Open three restaurants you own, all at once, to make a splash
options.feedback: Full control and a big launch. But you pay all the costs before you've learned anything, and three mistakes cost three times as much.

options.text: Open one flagship you own, run with a local operations partner
options.feedback: You keep control of quality and you learn directly. The partner shortens your learning curve on rent, staff and suppliers. Growth is slower at first.

options.text: Sell the rights for the whole country to a local restaurant group
options.feedback: Fast and cheap for you. But someone else controls your quality and keeps most of the learning, and that deal is hard to undo later.

cards.title: Say you opened one flagship. Locals like it, with notes.
body: Early guests love the dumplings. But many find the sauces too mild and the lunch portions small. What do you change?

options.text: Nothing. The menu is what made you successful
options.feedback: It protects your identity and keeps the kitchen simple. But you're ignoring a real taste gap, and guests may not come back.

options.text: Keep the signature dumplings identical; adapt sauces, portions and add one local special
options.feedback: The core that makes you different stays the same. The edges fit local habits. Your kitchen gets a little more complex.

options.text: Rebuild the menu around local favorites
options.feedback: It fits local tastes, but you lose what made you different. Now you're competing with local restaurants at their own game.

cards.softwareNote: Software works the same way. Keep the core product identical, and adapt the edges: language, payment methods, pricing levels and support hours.

cards.eyebrow: Decision 4 of 4 · Who you're up against
cards.title: Say you adapted the edges. Now, delivery.
body: At home, many orders come through your own app. Here, nobody has your app. One local delivery app dominates, and a local dumpling chain sits at the top of its rankings.

options.text: Launch your own app and skip the local delivery app
options.feedback: You keep the fees and the customer data. But you start with zero visibility, where the local chain already owns the screen.

options.text: List on the local app to get found, then invite repeat guests into your loyalty program
options.feedback: You meet customers where they already are, and slowly build a direct relationship. You pay platform fees and depend on its rules for a while.

options.text: List on the local app and price below the local chain
options.feedback: You may win clicks for a month. But the local chain has cheaper suppliers and loyal customers. A price war on its home turf is one you're likely to lose.

cards.title: What the best path looks like.
body: Not a triumph. A **foothold**: one profitable restaurant, a partner you trust, and real data about what travels and what doesn't.

breakdown.label: Flagship covers its costs
breakdown.detail: One restaurant, so losses stayed small while you learned

breakdown.label: Orders for the local special
breakdown.detail: The adapted edge pulls new guests in

cards.softwareNote: For an app, the same foothold might be one country with paying users, localized payments and a working support team, before you add the next language.

cards.title: The safe path has its own risks.
body: Starting close can make you overconfident. Success next door says little about a market that is far away in language, rules and taste.
A partner who knows the market also learns your business. Agree early on who owns what, including recipes and customer data.
And the delivery app that helped you get found can raise its fees. Keep building your direct relationship with customers, or your growth stays on someone else's terms.

cards.title: Going global is four linked decisions, not one big leap.
body: Each good choice lowered the risk of the next one. Here's how they map to this unit:
list: **Where:** pick a market close in culture, rules and geography first (*the distance between markets*)
**How:** enter in a way that lets you learn before you scale (*ways to enter a market*)
**What changes:** keep the core, adapt the edges (*localize or standardize*)
**Who you're up against:** don't fight local champions on their strengths (*local champions*)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick one market you'd like to enter. Write one sentence for each of the four decisions.
